youtube_title: They Copied a Rival's Phone Book — and Won at the Supreme Court 🦝⚖️
caption: Feist v. Rural (1991): copying phone listings wasn't copyright infringement, because facts aren't copyrightable and an alphabetical list isn't original. 'Copyright rewards originality, not effort.'
script: A company planted fake people in its phone book to catch a copycat. It caught them. Then it lost at the Supreme Court. [disclaimer] This is a real case from nineteen ninety one, Feist versus Rural Telephone. Rural Telephone was a phone company in Kansas, and it made a phone book. Feist made a bigger phone book and asked to use Rural's listings. Rural said no. So Feist just copied them anyway! More than a thousand listings. And get this. Four of those listings were fake! Rural had planted them on purpose to catch copycats. Busted, right? Rural sued for copyright, and won in the lower courts. But then the Supreme Court flipped it! Names, towns, and phone numbers are just facts. And the Court said you can't copyright facts. Ever! A list of facts is only protected if you made creative choices in picking them or arranging them. And putting names in A B C order? The Court said there's nothing creative about that at all. Ouch! The Court also said hard work alone doesn't earn a copyright. Copyright rewards being original, not just effort. Here's the limit. Original writing and creative choices can still be protected. Rural's phone book as a whole still had a copyright. And this isn't permission to copy whole websites. Privacy laws, contracts and site rules are a separate problem. [loop] So before you copy someone's phone book, remember

script_old: They copied a competitor's phone listings, and won at the Supreme Court. This is Feist versus Rural Telephone, from nineteen ninety-one. Rural Telephone, a utility in Kansas, published a phone book. Feist made bigger regional directories and asked to license Rural's white-pages listings. Rural said no. So Feist copied them anyway, one thousand three hundred nine listings. And four of those were fake listings Rural had planted to catch copiers. Caught red-handed, right? Rural sued for copyright infringement and won in the lower courts. But the Supreme Court reversed. Names, towns and phone numbers are facts. And copyright, the Court said, can never extend to the facts themselves. A collection of facts is protected only for original choices in selecting or arranging them, and the Court said there's nothing remotely creative about listing names alphabetically. It also rejected the idea that hard work alone earns a copyright. In its words, copyright rewards originality, not effort. Here's the limit. Original writing, and creative choices about what to include and how to arrange it, can still be protected. Rural's phone book as a whole still had a copyright. And this isn't permission to copy whole websites. Privacy laws, contracts and site terms are separate issues. [loop] So before you copy someone's phone book, remember
